M1.name: Token Intelligence in the Engineering Context
M1.learning_objective: Identify and classify input, output, and cache tokens and explain how token usage influences cost, latency, and quality in engineering workflows.
M1.core_mental_model: Tokens are not just text units; they are budget, latency, and reasoning-capacity constraints.
M1.in_scope: Token types, token cost basics, engineering impact, hidden token contributors, simple waste recognition.
M1.out_of_scope: Context engineering mechanics, MCP, memory systems, orchestration, advanced optimization patterns.
M1.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: label three token contributors in one recent interaction and estimate which one created the most waste.

concepts.name: Input Token
concepts.summary: An input token is any unit of text — word fragment, word, punctuation, space — sent to the model before it generates a response. Every character in a system prompt, user message, tool output, and conversation history becomes input tokens the model must process.
concepts.why_it_matters: Input tokens are the primary cost and latency driver. Every token in the prompt window costs money and adds processing time. Engineers who over-paste context or carry long histories pay for it on every request.
concepts.when_to_use: When calculating the cost of a prompt, when diagnosing why an API call is slow or expensive, when deciding what to include or exclude from a system prompt.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse with output tokens. Input tokens are consumed before generation begins.
concepts.example: An engineer pastes a 500-line service file into a prompt. Every line — including blank lines and comments — becomes input tokens the model charges for, even if only 20 lines are relevant.
concepts.non_example: Treating the prompt as free or zero-cost because it is 'just instructions'.

concepts.name: Output Token
concepts.summary: An output token is each unit of text the model generates in its response. Output tokens are metered separately from input tokens and typically cost more per token at most API pricing tiers.
concepts.why_it_matters: Verbose responses are not free. An engineer who receives a 2,000-token explanation when 200 tokens would suffice has paid 10x the necessary output cost — and added latency.
concepts.when_to_use: When reviewing model responses for verbosity, when setting output length constraints, when diagnosing why cost is higher than expected despite a short prompt.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not conflate with input tokens. Output tokens begin after the model starts generating, not before.
concepts.example: A model asked to 'review this function' returns a 40-paragraph essay including preamble, restated context, and a conclusion. Most of that is output token waste.
concepts.non_example: Assuming shorter prompts automatically mean shorter outputs. Output verbosity is controlled by instructions, not prompt length.

concepts.name: Cache Token
concepts.summary: Cache tokens are the saved computation from previously processed input that can be reused across requests. When the same prompt prefix appears repeatedly, the model can skip reprocessing it and use the cached key-value state instead.
concepts.why_it_matters: Prompt caching reduces cost and latency on repeated interactions — critical for production systems where a long system prompt is sent with every API call. Understanding caching helps engineers decide what to put in static vs dynamic parts of a prompt.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing system prompts for production agents, when the same large context is reused across many requests, when optimizing high-frequency API calls.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not assume caching is automatic or free — it requires correct prompt structure and supported API configurations.
concepts.example: A coding assistant has a 3,000-token system prompt defining its behaviour. With caching, this prefix is processed once and reused for all user turns — saving 3,000 input tokens per request.
concepts.non_example: Assuming every API call starts fresh with zero cost savings. Caching is not the same as storing data — it is saved computation state.

concepts.name: KV Cache
concepts.summary: The KV (key-value) cache stores the intermediate attention computations produced when the model processes input tokens. These stored values allow the model to skip recomputing attention over already-seen tokens on subsequent turns.
concepts.why_it_matters: KV cache is why context accumulation has a compounding latency cost. Each new turn adds tokens that must either be recomputed or retrieved from cache. Engineers building multi-turn systems need to understand this to design efficient session architectures.
concepts.when_to_use: When reasoning about why longer sessions get progressively slower, when designing multi-turn workflows, when evaluating whether to reset context or carry it.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse with application-level data caching. KV cache is internal to the model inference process.
concepts.example: In a 10-turn conversation, the model builds up KV cache over earlier turns. By turn 10, retrieving cached attention is faster than recomputing — but a bloated history with tool outputs and repeated instructions fills the cache with low-value computation.
concepts.non_example: Thinking about KV cache as a feature the engineer configures directly. It is an internal model mechanism, not an API setting.

concepts.name: Tokenization Boundary
concepts.summary: Tokenization boundaries are the points at which text is split into tokens. These boundaries do not align with word or sentence boundaries — they depend on the model's tokenizer, language, and character patterns. Code, punctuation, whitespace, and non-English text tokenize differently from English prose.
concepts.why_it_matters: Engineers who assume one word equals one token will systematically underestimate token counts. Code is particularly expensive to tokenize — symbols, indentation, and variable names each consume tokens at rates higher than prose.
concepts.when_to_use: When estimating prompt cost, when comparing token counts across languages, when evaluating whether to include code snippets or summaries.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not use word count as a token proxy. Always use a tokenizer tool for accurate counts.
concepts.example: The phrase 'context engineering' may tokenize as ['context', ' engineering'] — 2 tokens. But a line of Python code like 'def calculate_total(items):' may tokenize into 8 or more tokens due to symbols and spacing.
concepts.non_example: Counting words in a prompt and multiplying by a fixed ratio. Tokenization is language and content specific.

concepts.name: Token Cost
concepts.summary: Token cost is the economic and computational price of each token processed in an API call. Input and output tokens are priced separately. Token cost accumulates across every turn, every session, and every user — making it a first-order engineering concern in production systems.
concepts.why_it_matters: Token cost is not a billing footnote — it is an architecture constraint. At scale, the difference between a well-curated 500-token prompt and a bloated 5,000-token prompt is a 10x cost difference on every API call.
concepts.when_to_use: When sizing API budgets, when comparing architecture options, when reviewing prompts and skill files for cost efficiency.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not optimise for token count at the expense of relevance. Removing necessary context to save tokens creates worse outputs that require more retries — which costs more.
concepts.example: A team's AI feature costs £0.002 per request at 500 tokens. At 10,000 daily requests that is £20/day. A 3x bloated prompt increases this to £60/day — £14,600/year in waste.
concepts.non_example: Treating token cost as an infrastructure cost invisible to engineers. In production, token cost is as real as compute cost.

concepts.name: Latency Scaling
concepts.summary: Latency scales with token count. Processing more input tokens takes longer before generation begins. Generating more output tokens takes longer to complete. In multi-turn sessions, accumulated context adds latency at every turn — not just the first.
concepts.why_it_matters: For user-facing engineering tools, latency above 3–5 seconds feels broken. Token-driven latency is invisible in testing but compounds in production at scale and multi-turn depth.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing real-time or interactive engineering workflows, when setting performance SLAs, when diagnosing why a feature feels slow in production.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse with network latency. Token processing latency is model-side and scales with prompt size.
concepts.example: An IDE assistant that loads the entire codebase as context takes 8 seconds to respond. The same assistant using scoped file reads responds in 1.5 seconds — same model, same task, different token count.
concepts.non_example: Blaming network speed for slow responses when the real issue is a 10,000-token prompt that takes 4 seconds to process before the model generates a single word.

concepts.name: Visible Token Contributor
concepts.summary: Visible token contributors are the prompt elements an engineer can see and consciously control: the user message, pasted code, file contents, and explicit system instructions. These are the tokens most engineers focus on when thinking about prompt size.
concepts.why_it_matters: Visible contributors are the starting point for token awareness, but they are not the whole story. Focusing only on visible contributors causes engineers to miss the hidden contributors that often dominate cost and latency.
concepts.when_to_use: When auditing prompt content, when deciding what to include or summarise, when trimming obvious bloat.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not assume visible contributors are the primary waste driver. Hidden contributors often exceed visible ones in multi-turn sessions.
concepts.example: An engineer copies a 200-line file into a prompt. They can see and count those 200 lines. That is a visible contributor — they know it is there and can choose to summarise it instead.
concepts.non_example: Thinking that reviewing the user message and pasted code covers all token optimisation. Hidden contributors are invisible by definition.

concepts.name: Hidden Token Contributor
concepts.summary: Hidden token contributors are prompt elements that consume tokens without the engineer consciously noticing: accumulated conversation history, repeated system instructions, tool output payloads, intermediate reasoning traces, and retry accumulation from failed attempts.
concepts.why_it_matters: Hidden contributors are often the largest waste source in production systems. Engineers fix visible contributors and wonder why cost and latency stay high — the hidden contributors were always the real problem.
concepts.when_to_use: When diagnosing unexpectedly high token counts, when reviewing multi-turn session logs, when auditing tool output handling.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not ignore hidden contributors when optimising. Trimming visible content while leaving hidden accumulation unchanged produces minimal improvement.
concepts.example: A debugging session runs 8 turns. Each turn carries the full prior conversation, two tool output payloads from earlier turns, and the repeated system prompt. The visible user message is 50 tokens. The hidden contributors are 4,000 tokens.
concepts.non_example: Treating conversation history as free. Every prior turn sitting in context is a hidden token contributor paid for on every subsequent request.

concepts.name: Token Budget Mental Model
concepts.summary: The token budget mental model treats the model's context window as a fixed budget — not an unlimited space. Every token included is a deliberate allocation. Every unnecessary token is waste that crowds out useful information and inflates cost.
concepts.why_it_matters: Engineers who think of context as 'the bigger the better' consistently overpay and get worse results. Engineers who think of context as a budget allocate tokens to the information that most improves the answer.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing prompts, instruction files, and skill files. When reviewing any artifact that will be processed by a model repeatedly.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not apply token budget thinking so aggressively that necessary context is removed. The goal is relevance, not minimalism.
concepts.example: A test architecture review prompt allocates: 200 tokens for role/persona, 300 tokens for specific task context, 100 tokens for output format. Every other token is cut. Result: faster, cheaper, more focused responses.
concepts.non_example: Treating a 128,000 token context window as permission to fill it. A large window is a safety net, not an invitation.

misconceptions.misconception: Tokens are just words
misconceptions.why_wrong: Tokenization does not align with word boundaries. A single word can be multiple tokens; punctuation, spaces, and code symbols each consume tokens independently.
misconceptions.correct_view: A token is a sub-word unit produced by a tokenizer. Word count is an unreliable proxy for token count — especially for code, punctuation, and non-English text.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I counted the words in my prompt — it is only 200 words so it should be cheap.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If tokens were just words, what would happen when the model processes a line of Python code with 10 symbols and no words?' Guide toward tokenizer mechanics.

misconceptions.misconception: More tokens always improve performance
misconceptions.why_wrong: Attention is not uniform — the model does not benefit equally from all tokens. Past a threshold, additional tokens dilute relevance and cause the model to deweight important context.
misconceptions.correct_view: Token quality matters more than token quantity. A well-curated 500-token prompt often outperforms a bloated 5,000-token prompt on the same task.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I should give the model as much context as possible — more is always better.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If more tokens always helped, why do long sessions often produce worse results than short, focused ones?' Probe the attention dilution concept.

misconceptions.misconception: Token limits only matter at the hard maximum
misconceptions.why_wrong: Quality degradation and cost accumulation begin well before the hard context limit. In practice, performance and economics suffer long before the window is full.
misconceptions.correct_view: Token management is relevant throughout the session, not just as an emergency measure when approaching the limit.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'We have a 128k context window — we do not need to worry about tokens until we get close to the limit.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What happens to cost and latency if every request uses 50k tokens when 5k would suffice?' Guide toward the economic and quality argument.

misconceptions.misconception: Cache tokens are free
misconceptions.why_wrong: Cache tokens reduce reprocessing cost but are not zero-cost. Cache hits save computation but the original caching incurs cost, and cache misses result in full reprocessing.
misconceptions.correct_view: Prompt caching is a cost-reduction mechanism, not a cost-elimination mechanism. It requires correct prompt structure and has its own pricing model.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'We use prompt caching so tokens do not matter for our system prompt.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What happens when the cache misses — does caching eliminate processing cost entirely?' Surface the conditional nature of caching.

misconceptions.misconception: Output tokens are less important than input tokens
misconceptions.why_wrong: Output tokens are typically priced higher per token than input tokens at most API tiers. A verbose output is often more expensive than the prompt that generated it.
misconceptions.correct_view: Both input and output tokens carry significant cost. Output verbosity is a major and often overlooked cost driver.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'The prompt is the main cost — the response is just what comes back.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If a model generates a 3,000-token response to a 500-token prompt, which is likely more expensive?' Surface the pricing asymmetry.

socratic_bank.prompt: What happens to your prompt before the model generates a single word?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening question to surface token processing awareness
socratic_bank.expected_response: Model reads and processes it / it costs something / it gets converted
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What specifically gets converted, and what is each unit of that conversion called?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Think about the journey from text to model output — what step happens first before any response appears?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Imagine the model as a reader. What does it have to do with every character you send before it can reply?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You pasted a 300-line file and a 10-word question. Which part do you think costs more to process?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner identifies input tokens exist
socratic_bank.expected_response: The file / both / not sure
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Now think about the response the model gives back — is that counted in the same way?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What makes the file more expensive — is it the number of characters, the number of words, or something else?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If you had to pay for every unit the model reads, which of these two inputs would your bill be higher for?'

socratic_bank.prompt: If tokens were just words, what would happen when the model processes a Python function?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner understands tokens are text units
socratic_bank.expected_response: Code has symbols that are not words / it would undercount / not sure
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So what does that tell you about using word count as your token estimate?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Think about a line like def calculate_total(items): — how many words is that, and how might the tokenizer treat each symbol?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What is in a line of code besides words? How might each of those elements be counted?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said more context always helps. What happens to a model when it receives 100,000 tokens of mixed-relevance content?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner claims more context is always better
socratic_bank.expected_response: It might get confused / not all of it is equally useful / it attends to all of it
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So what is the difference between more context and better context?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'If the model attends to everything equally, what happens to the one relevant paragraph buried in 100k tokens?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Think about reading a 500-page book to answer one specific question — is more pages always more helpful?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us take a step back. Tell me what you think the difference is between what you type and what the model processes.
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner is confused about token basics — recovery question
socratic_bank.expected_response: Some awareness that conversion happens
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good — what do you think that conversion step is called?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'When you type a message, the model does not see letters — it sees something else. What might that be?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Think about how a computer represents text internally. What do you know about that?'

M2.name: The Evolution from Prompting to Context Engineering
M2.learning_objective: Explain why prompt engineering fails at scale and distinguish prompting from context engineering in multi-turn, tool-assisted systems.
M2.core_mental_model: Prompting is a local optimization; context engineering is whole-system control of information visibility and timing.
M2.in_scope: Prompt vs context distinction, lifecycle, accumulation, drift, system-thinking transition.
M2.out_of_scope: MCP mechanics, deep tool orchestration, memory architecture, advanced optimization, Copilot Studio configuration details.
M2.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: list every context element that influenced one multi-turn engineering interaction beyond the initial prompt.

concepts.name: Prompt Engineering
concepts.summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting, tuning, and iterating on a single prompt to improve the model's response to a specific query. It is local optimisation — focused on what is said in one request at one moment.
concepts.why_it_matters: Prompt engineering is a valuable starting skill, but it does not scale to multi-turn, tool-assisted, or stateful workflows. Understanding its limits is the first step toward context engineering.
concepts.when_to_use: When handling one-shot or single-turn tasks. When the task is well-defined, self-contained, and does not depend on prior state.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not rely on prompt engineering alone for multi-turn workflows, agentic systems, or tasks where history and tool outputs accumulate across turns.
concepts.example: Writing a prompt that asks a model to 'review this function for security vulnerabilities, output findings as a bullet list, cite line numbers' — that is prompt engineering. It works well for a single, self-contained request.
concepts.non_example: Treating every interaction as a prompt engineering problem. When a workflow involves five turns, tool calls, and accumulated history, the prompt is only one element — not the system.

concepts.name: Context Engineering
concepts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of designing and managing everything the model sees across an entire interaction — system instructions, user messages, tool outputs, history, retrieved documents, and state — so that the right information is available at the right moment in the right amount.
concepts.why_it_matters: As AI workflows move from one-shot prompts to multi-turn agents, the quality of the context design determines the quality of the outcome. A brilliant prompt in a broken context still fails.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing multi-turn workflows, agents, or any system where more than one message is exchanged with the model.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Context engineering does not replace prompt engineering — it includes it. Do not abandon prompt craft; extend it to the whole system.
concepts.example: A code review agent is context-engineered to: load only the changed files (not the whole repo), carry the PR description as persistent context, retrieve the team's coding standards on demand, and reset tool output after each file review. Each of these is a context engineering decision.
concepts.non_example: Thinking context engineering means writing a longer system prompt. Context engineering is about what is included, excluded, ordered, and timed — not about size.

concepts.name: Context State
concepts.summary: Context state is the complete set of information currently available to the model at any point in an interaction — everything in its visible window. Context state includes the system prompt, all prior messages, any tool outputs, and any retrieved content loaded into the session.
concepts.why_it_matters: Context state is dynamic — it grows with every turn. Engineers who do not actively manage context state find that it drifts, accumulates waste, and eventually degrades the model's ability to stay on task.
concepts.when_to_use: When auditing what the model actually sees at a given turn. When diagnosing why a multi-turn workflow is producing inconsistent or drifting responses.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse context state with the user's intent or the task description. Context state is what the model sees — not what the engineer meant.
concepts.example: At turn 5 of a debugging session, the context state contains: the original system prompt, four prior user messages, four prior model responses, two tool outputs from earlier turns, and a retrieved error log. That is the full state the model reasons from.
concepts.non_example: Assuming the model reasons only from the latest message. Every prior turn in the window is part of the state the model attends to.

concepts.name: Context Lifecycle
concepts.summary: The context lifecycle describes how context state changes over the duration of an interaction: it starts with the system prompt, grows with each user turn and model response, expands further with tool outputs and retrieved content, and must be actively pruned or reset to avoid degradation.
concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding the lifecycle prevents engineers from treating context as static. A prompt that works at turn 1 may fail at turn 10 because the lifecycle has filled the context with noise that drowns out the signal.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing multi-turn workflows. When deciding where to prune, reset, or summarise context. When debugging why a long session produces worse results than a short one.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not treat the context lifecycle as an automatic process. It requires deliberate design — what enters, when it enters, and when it leaves.
concepts.example: Turn 1: system prompt + user task = clean context. Turn 3: + two model responses + one tool output. Turn 6: + further accumulation. Without pruning, the signal-to-noise ratio drops continuously across the lifecycle.
concepts.non_example: Thinking of context as a fixed container that stays the same across turns. Context is a living, growing state that degrades if unmanaged.

concepts.name: Prompt Drift
concepts.summary: Prompt drift occurs when accumulated context causes the model to gradually deviate from its original task instructions. Earlier constraints are diluted by subsequent messages, tool outputs, and clarifications until the model no longer consistently applies the original rules.
concepts.why_it_matters: Prompt drift is one of the most common failure modes in long-running engineering workflows. It is invisible until the output is noticeably wrong — which may be many turns after the drift began.
concepts.when_to_use: When reviewing multi-turn conversations for consistency. When a model that worked correctly at the start begins producing inconsistent or rule-violating outputs later in the session.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse prompt drift with model error. Drift is caused by context management failure, not model capability.
concepts.example: An architecture review agent is instructed at turn 1 to always flag security risks. By turn 8, accumulated conversation about performance and code style has pushed the security instruction deep into the context. The model stops flagging security risks — not because it forgot, but because security is now a small signal in a noisy context.
concepts.non_example: Assuming the model will always follow turn-1 instructions regardless of what accumulates later. Models attend to the full context — earlier instructions can be overwhelmed by later content.

misconceptions.misconception: A good enough prompt scales to any workflow
misconceptions.why_wrong: Prompt quality is one input to a multi-turn system. At scale, conversation history, tool outputs, clarifications, and accumulated state interact in ways no single prompt can control.
misconceptions.correct_view: Prompting is local optimisation. Context engineering is system-level design. They are not substitutes — one operates at the level of a message, the other at the level of the whole workflow.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'If I just write a really good system prompt, everything else will work.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What changes between turn 1 and turn 8 of a conversation, even if the system prompt stays the same?' Guide toward context accumulation.

misconceptions.misconception: Context is just a bigger prompt
misconceptions.why_wrong: Context includes history, tool outputs, retrieved documents, and dynamic state — elements that do not exist in a static prompt. Managing context requires different skills than writing prompts.
misconceptions.correct_view: Context is a living, changing system. A prompt is a static artifact. Context engineering manages the whole system across time.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'Context engineering is just prompt engineering with a longer system prompt.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What elements of a multi-turn interaction cannot be addressed by writing a better system prompt?' Surface history, tools, and state.

misconceptions.misconception: History always helps
misconceptions.why_wrong: Past conversation history is only useful if it contains relevant, non-redundant information. Accumulated history often contains clarifications, retries, and tangents that dilute the current task's signal.
misconceptions.correct_view: History is selectively useful. Relevant history helps; irrelevant history hurts. Context engineering decides which history to carry and which to prune.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'Keep the full conversation history — the model needs to remember everything.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If a 10-turn conversation includes 3 turns about a now-resolved misunderstanding, does carrying those turns help or hurt the model on turn 11?'

misconceptions.misconception: Repeating instructions equals context engineering
misconceptions.why_wrong: Restating the same instruction every turn is a symptom of poor context engineering — it adds token cost without fixing the underlying issue of instruction drift. Context engineering addresses why instructions drift, not by repeating them.
misconceptions.correct_view: Context engineering manages the conditions that cause drift — including what accumulates in the context — rather than compensating for drift by repetition.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I just restate the key rules at the start of every message to make sure the model follows them.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What is the token cost of restating 500 words of instructions on every turn across 100 engineers? And does restatement prevent drift or just paper over it?'

misconceptions.misconception: Prompt drift is a model bug
misconceptions.why_wrong: Prompt drift is caused by context accumulation diluting earlier instructions — it is a context management failure, not a model defect. The model is attending to everything in context; the problem is that the signal is being overwhelmed by noise.
misconceptions.correct_view: Prompt drift is an engineering problem with an engineering solution: prune irrelevant history, reinforce critical constraints structurally, and design context so core instructions remain prominent.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'The model keeps forgetting my instructions — it must be a reliability issue with the model.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If you cleared the conversation history and started fresh, would the model follow the instructions again?' If yes, the issue is context accumulation, not model reliability.

socratic_bank.prompt: A prompt works perfectly at turn 1. By turn 8 it stops following your instructions. What changed?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening question to surface context accumulation awareness
socratic_bank.expected_response: Something accumulated / the conversation got long / not sure
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What specifically accumulated — what is sitting in the context at turn 8 that was not there at turn 1?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'If the instructions are the same, what else might be influencing the model at turn 8?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Is the model at turn 8 seeing only the latest message, or everything since turn 1?'

socratic_bank.prompt: What elements are in the model's context at turn 5 that were not there at turn 1?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner understands something accumulates
socratic_bank.expected_response: Prior messages / responses / tool outputs
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'And how does the model treat all of those elements — does it focus on the latest message or attend to everything?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Think about what happens after each turn — what new content enters the context?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What did the model generate in response to turns 1 through 4? Where does that go?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said you would write a better prompt to fix the drift. Would a better prompt change what accumulates in context after 8 turns?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner defaults to prompt rewriting as the fix
socratic_bank.expected_response: No / maybe not / it depends
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So what would actually need to change to prevent instructions from drifting after 8 turns?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'The prompt is turn 1's contribution to context. What is contributing to context at turns 2 through 8?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If the problem is caused by accumulation, is the solution to change what you put in — or to manage what accumulates?'

socratic_bank.prompt: What is the difference between what you said in the prompt and what the model sees when generating the turn 8 response?
socratic_bank.use_when: To surface the difference between prompt and context state
socratic_bank.expected_response: The model sees more than just the prompt / it sees the full history
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So when we talk about controlling what the model responds to, are we controlling the prompt or something larger?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'At turn 8, is the model reading only your latest message?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What would you see if you could look at the model's full input at turn 8?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us simplify. Imagine you are having a conversation and all previous messages are read aloud before each reply. How does that change what influences the response?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner cannot grasp context accumulation
socratic_bank.expected_response: Earlier messages influence the response / everything said matters
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Now apply that to the model — does it work the same way?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What happens to the influence of your original instructions as more messages are read aloud?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Confirm the analogy is landing and then ask: 'So the model at turn 8 is influenced by how many prior messages?'

M3.name: Context Engineering — What It Is and How It Works
M3.learning_objective: Analyze context composition using the three-bloat model and explain how context design choices affect token cost and answer quality.
M3.core_mental_model: Context is an actively curated working state; quality depends on what is excluded as much as what is included.
M3.in_scope: Three-bloat model; context architecture; symptom-to-cause reasoning.
M3.out_of_scope: Deep MCP implementation, graph memory, runtime orchestration.
M3.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: classify one saturated session into input, output, and session bloat and name one thing to remove.

concepts.name: Input Bloat
concepts.summary: Input bloat is unnecessary content loaded into the context before the model generates a response. It includes overly long system prompts, pasted files that are larger than needed, repeated instructions, and retrieved documents that are not relevant to the current task.
concepts.why_it_matters: Input bloat inflates cost before a single output token is generated. It also dilutes the signal — useful content competes with noise for the model's attention.
concepts.when_to_use: When reviewing system prompts, skill files, and instruction files. When deciding whether to paste a full file or a relevant excerpt.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not confuse input bloat with having a long prompt. A long prompt with only relevant content is not bloat. Bloat is unnecessary length.
concepts.example: An instruction file includes the full company onboarding documentation, three versions of the coding standards, and a FAQ section that is never relevant to the agent's task. All of it loads on every request — that is input bloat.
concepts.non_example: Thinking every word in the system prompt is necessary because 'more context is always better'. Context engineering is about curation, not maximalism.

concepts.name: Output Bloat
concepts.summary: Output bloat is low-value verbosity in the model's generated response: preambles ('Great question! Let me explain...'), restated context, ceremonial summaries, excessive caveats, and padding that adds length without adding information.
concepts.why_it_matters: Output bloat wastes money on output tokens, increases latency, and buries the useful content in noise. In agentic systems, bloated output also becomes the next turn's input — compounding the cost.
concepts.when_to_use: When reviewing model responses for unnecessary length. When setting output constraints in skill files and instruction files. When diagnosing why responses feel slow or hard to parse.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not remove useful explanation to eliminate output bloat. The goal is removing padding, not removing substance.
concepts.example: A model asked 'which test failed?' responds with: 'That is a great question. Let me walk you through my analysis of your test suite. Based on a thorough review of the output you provided, I can confirm that...' before eventually naming the failing test. The preamble is output bloat.
concepts.non_example: Treating a longer answer as a better answer. In engineering workflows, precision and brevity are quality signals.

concepts.name: Session Bloat
concepts.summary: Session bloat is the accumulation of context across conversation turns that is no longer needed but continues to be carried: prior model responses, earlier tool outputs, superseded clarifications, and redundant retry attempts.
concepts.why_it_matters: Session bloat grows invisibly. Unlike input or output bloat, it is not visible in any single message — it accumulates across turns. By turn 10, a session can be carrying thousands of tokens of stale content that dilutes relevance and drives up cost.
concepts.when_to_use: When auditing multi-turn sessions for accumulated waste. When deciding whether to prune history, summarise prior turns, or reset context.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not remove session content that is still actively relevant. Not all session history is bloat — only the content that no longer contributes to the current task.
concepts.example: A 12-turn debugging session carries: 6 prior model responses (many now irrelevant), 4 tool outputs from earlier steps (already acted on), and 3 restatements of the same error message. None of this is needed for the current turn — it is session bloat.
concepts.non_example: Treating conversation history as sacred. History is useful until it is not — and session bloat is what happens when no one prunes it.

concepts.name: Always-Load Architecture
concepts.summary: Always-load refers to content that should be present in every request because it is universally needed: core role definition, safety constraints, and the fundamental task framing. Always-load content is the stable backbone of the context.
concepts.why_it_matters: Identifying what truly belongs in always-load prevents two failure modes: loading too much (bloat) and loading too little (the model lacks critical context). Always-load should be the minimum necessary for consistent behaviour.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing system prompts and instruction files. When deciding which guidelines, rules, or context elements should be permanent versus conditional.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not default to always-load for everything. Most content is better served by on-demand or never-load approaches.
concepts.example: A code review agent always loads: its role definition (500 tokens), the team's non-negotiable security rules (200 tokens), and the output format spec (100 tokens). Total: 800 tokens. Everything else is loaded on demand.
concepts.non_example: Pasting the entire coding standards document into every request because 'the model might need it'. If a rule is only relevant for specific file types, it belongs in on-demand, not always-load.

concepts.name: On-Demand Architecture
concepts.summary: On-demand refers to content that is retrieved and loaded only when the current task requires it: specific file contents, reference documents, tool results for the active step, and context that is conditionally relevant.
concepts.why_it_matters: On-demand loading is the primary mechanism for keeping context lean across varied tasks. Instead of loading everything that might be relevant, the system loads only what the current task needs.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing agents that handle varied tasks. When deciding whether to include a document in the static context or retrieve it conditionally. When using RAG or tool-based retrieval.
concepts.when_not_to_use: On-demand loading requires the ability to detect what is needed and retrieve it at the right time. It does not work without a retrieval mechanism.
concepts.example: A documentation agent retrieves only the specific API reference pages relevant to the engineer's current question, rather than loading the full API documentation on every request.
concepts.non_example: Fetching everything on first load 'just in case'. On-demand architecture requires the discipline to not pre-load speculatively.

misconceptions.misconception: All bloat is the same problem
misconceptions.why_wrong: Input, output, and session bloat have different causes, different symptoms, and different fixes. Treating them as one problem leads to fixes that address the wrong type.
misconceptions.correct_view: The three bloat types are distinct. Input bloat is about what goes in before generation. Output bloat is about what the model generates. Session bloat is about what accumulates across turns.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I have a token problem — I just need to reduce the amount of text.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If you shortened the prompt but the session history kept growing, would the problem be solved?' Force separation of the three types.

misconceptions.misconception: Bigger context windows eliminate curation needs
misconceptions.why_wrong: Larger context windows increase capacity but do not improve attention quality. A model with a 200k token window still attends non-uniformly — content buried in a large context receives less reliable attention than content in a focused context.
misconceptions.correct_view: Context curation is necessary regardless of window size. The purpose of curation is not to avoid hitting the limit — it is to ensure the model attends to the right things.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'We moved to a 200k token model — we do not need to worry about context design anymore.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If you put a single relevant sentence in 200k tokens of noise, would the model reliably find it?' Surface the attention quality argument.

misconceptions.misconception: Verbose output is harmless
misconceptions.why_wrong: In agentic systems, output becomes input for the next step. A verbose 2,000-token response that could have been 200 tokens will add 1,800 tokens of unnecessary input cost to every subsequent turn that carries it.
misconceptions.correct_view: Output verbosity compounds in multi-turn systems. It is a cost at the turn it occurs and a bloat driver for all subsequent turns.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'The model is just being thorough — long answers are fine, we are not paying by the word.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'In an agent pipeline where the response of step 3 becomes part of the context for step 4, what is the true cost of a response that is 10x longer than needed?'

socratic_bank.prompt: This session is slow and the outputs are drifting. Before we fix anything — what do you want to understand first?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening diagnostic question for Module 3
socratic_bank.expected_response: Where the tokens are going / what is causing the problem / what type of bloat it is
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good — so what would you look at to understand where the tokens are going?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What information would help you decide which part of the session to fix?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Think about the three stages of a session — before generation, during generation, and across turns. Which one would you check first?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Which part of this session existed before the model generated a single word?
socratic_bank.use_when: To separate input from output and session bloat
socratic_bank.expected_response: The system prompt / the user messages / the pasted files
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good — and what do we call it when there is more of that than needed?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Think about everything that was in the context window before generation began — what is that category?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'The model reads something before it writes something. What did it read in this session?'

socratic_bank.prompt: A coding assistant carries the full conversation history across 15 turns. Which bloat type is accumulating?
socratic_bank.use_when: To test classification of session bloat specifically
socratic_bank.expected_response: Session bloat
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What would happen to the input token count at turn 15 compared to turn 1 if full history is always carried?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Is the accumulation happening before generation, during generation, or across turns over time?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Think about when this content enters the context — is it there from the start, created by the model, or built up over multiple exchanges?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said the context window is large so curation is not needed. What happens to the model's attention when 100k of a 128k window is filled with low-relevance content?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner invokes large context window as excuse not to curate
socratic_bank.expected_response: Attention is diluted / the relevant content gets lost / not sure
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So what is the purpose of context curation — is it about avoiding the limit or about something else?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'If the model attends non-uniformly, what happens to a 200-token relevant section buried in 90k tokens of background?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Is a 128k token window permission to fill it, or a safety net for exceptional cases?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us sort the session artifacts into three bins: what was there before the model started, what the model created, and what built up across turns. Which bin is biggest?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner cannot classify bloat types
socratic_bank.expected_response: Some awareness of the three categories
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What do we call waste in each of those three bins?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Help learner name the bins (input, output, session) and then ask: 'In this specific session, which bin is contributing the most tokens?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Walk through one artifact together: 'Where does the pasted file go — which bin? Where does the model response go? Where does the prior conversation go?'

M4.name: Diagnosing Token Cost
M4.learning_objective: Interpret debug console outputs or token breakdowns, identify dominant waste patterns, and recommend the highest-ROI fix with defensible reasoning.
M4.core_mental_model: You cannot optimize what you have not correctly diagnosed.
M4.in_scope: Token traces, cause-vs-symptom logic, one-fix prioritization.
M4.out_of_scope: Broader optimization frameworks, memory redesign, full agent architecture.
M4.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: name the dominant bloat, likely cause, and one highest-ROI fix—nothing more.

concepts.name: Dominant Bloat Pattern
concepts.summary: The dominant bloat pattern is the single largest source of waste in a specific session — the bloat type (input, output, or session) that is contributing most to excess tokens, cost, or latency degradation. Correct identification of the dominant pattern is the prerequisite for effective optimisation.
concepts.why_it_matters: Fixing the wrong bloat type produces minimal improvement. Engineers who optimise output verbosity when session accumulation is the dominant issue will see little change — because they fixed the secondary problem.
concepts.when_to_use: When beginning any token optimisation task. Always identify dominant bloat before recommending a fix.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not assume the most visible problem is the dominant one. The largest visible artifact is often not the largest token consumer.
concepts.example: A debug session shows: input tokens 800, output tokens 1,200, but session history has grown to 6,000 tokens across 10 turns. The dominant bloat is session bloat — not output verbosity, even though the output looks long.
concepts.non_example: Jumping to output trimming as the default fix for every token problem. Output is often the most visible contributor but rarely the dominant one in mature multi-turn sessions.

concepts.name: Evidence-First Diagnosis
concepts.summary: Evidence-first diagnosis is the discipline of reading token counts, trends, and trace data before forming a hypothesis about waste. It prevents engineers from treating the most emotionally obvious symptom as the root cause.
concepts.why_it_matters: Without evidence-first reasoning, optimisation is guesswork. Engineers fix what bothers them aesthetically (verbose output, long prompts) rather than what the data shows is costing the most.
concepts.when_to_use: At the start of every token diagnosis task. Before recommending any optimisation fix.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not skip evidence review because the problem 'looks obvious'. The obvious problem is often a symptom of a less visible cause.
concepts.example: An engineer sees a verbose model response and immediately wants to add output length constraints. Evidence-first diagnosis reveals that the output is 800 tokens but the session history is 12,000 tokens — the right fix is session pruning, not output trimming.
concepts.non_example: Starting with a fix before reading the token breakdown. Diagnosis must precede prescription.

concepts.name: Highest-ROI Fix
concepts.summary: The highest-ROI fix is the single change most likely to reduce waste materially without harming answer quality or relevance. It is chosen based on evidence — not intuition, preference, or ease of implementation.
concepts.why_it_matters: In any optimisation scenario, multiple fixes are possible. Choosing the highest-ROI fix means the engineer gets the maximum benefit from one intervention, rather than making several low-value changes that collectively do less.
concepts.when_to_use: When a diagnosis is complete and a fix must be recommended. Always choose one fix and justify it over alternatives.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not recommend a list of fixes. The discipline of Module 4 is prioritisation — one fix, one reason, one expected outcome.
concepts.example: Session bloat is the dominant pattern (8,000 tokens of history). Highest-ROI fix: summarise prior turns after every 3 exchanges, reducing session tokens by ~70%. Alternative fixes (trim output, shorten system prompt) would each save <200 tokens — far lower ROI.
concepts.non_example: Recommending five changes simultaneously. A fix list signals diagnosis failure — the engineer has not prioritised.

concepts.name: Root Cause vs Symptom
concepts.summary: The root cause of token waste is the operational pattern that generates the waste. The symptom is the visible manifestation — high token count, slow response, drifting output. Confusing symptom for cause leads to fixes that do not hold.
concepts.why_it_matters: Treating symptoms produces temporary improvements. An engineer who trims a verbose response has addressed the symptom. The engineer who identifies that verbose output is caused by an absence of output format constraints in the skill file has addressed the root cause.
concepts.when_to_use: When explaining a diagnosis. Always name both the symptom and the cause separately.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not stop at naming the symptom. The symptom is the starting point, not the destination.
concepts.example: Symptom: model response is 2,000 tokens when 200 would suffice. Root cause: the skill file has no output format constraint and no brevity instruction — the model defaults to maximum elaboration.
concepts.non_example: Writing 'the output is too long' as a diagnosis. That is the symptom. The cause is an instruction architecture gap.

concepts.name: Token Trend Reading
concepts.summary: Token trend reading is the practice of looking at how token counts change across turns in a session — not just the total at one moment. Rising input tokens across turns indicate session accumulation. Stable input with rising output suggests verbosity drift. Spikes indicate large tool payload injection.
concepts.why_it_matters: A single snapshot of token counts can be misleading. Trends reveal whether a problem is growing (accumulation), fixed (one-time overload), or intermittent (triggered by specific actions). Trend reading enables targeted fixes.
concepts.when_to_use: When reviewing multi-turn debug logs or token analytics. When diagnosing a problem that appears to worsen over time rather than being present from the start.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not read only the latest turn's token count. The trend across turns often tells a different story than any single measurement.
concepts.example: Turn 1: 1,200 input tokens. Turn 3: 2,800. Turn 5: 4,900. Turn 7: 7,200. The rising trend confirms session accumulation — each turn carries all prior content. The fix is history pruning, not prompt shortening.
concepts.non_example: Looking only at the most recent request's token count and concluding the prompt is too long. The latest prompt might be short — the history is what is growing.

misconceptions.misconception: The most visible artifact is the biggest problem
misconceptions.why_wrong: The most visible artifact — often a long pasted file or a verbose response — draws attention disproportionately. The dominant token consumer is often invisible: accumulated history, repeated tool outputs, or hidden retry context.
misconceptions.correct_view: Evidence-first diagnosis reveals the actual dominant pattern. Visible salience is not the same as quantitative dominance.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'The problem is obvious — that pasted file is huge. Cut it down.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'Before we fix the pasted file, let us read the token breakdown. What does the session history contribute across all turns? Is the file actually the dominant cost?'

misconceptions.misconception: More fixes are always better
misconceptions.why_wrong: Multiple simultaneous fixes obscure which change actually worked and make it impossible to learn from the intervention. Module 4 trains prioritisation — one fix, one measurement, one learning.
misconceptions.correct_view: The highest-ROI fix, applied alone, produces clearer learning and often more improvement than several lower-ROI fixes applied together.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I will try trimming the output, shortening the prompt, and pruning the history all at once.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If you make three changes simultaneously and the problem improves, how will you know which change was responsible? If it gets worse, which change caused it?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Here is a token breakdown: input 900, output 1,100, session history growing by 800 tokens per turn across 10 turns. What do you notice first?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening diagnostic question with numbers
socratic_bank.expected_response: The session history is the largest and growing / the total is high / not sure
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What does a trend of +800 tokens per turn across 10 turns tell you about the dominant problem?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Which of these three numbers would you expect to be highest by turn 20 if nothing changes?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Before deciding what to fix, what does each number tell you about where the tokens are coming from?'

socratic_bank.prompt: What is the difference between the visible symptom and the operational cause in this trace?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner identifies a pattern
socratic_bank.expected_response: Symptom is the high token count / cause is what is generating it
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good — so if the symptom is rising tokens, what is the operational action that is causing the session history to grow?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Can you name the symptom in one sentence and the cause in a separate sentence?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What would have to stop happening for the session history to stop growing?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You have identified session accumulation as the dominant pattern. Of the three things you could fix, which one would reduce tokens most per request?
socratic_bank.use_when: After dominant pattern is correctly identified
socratic_bank.expected_response: Pruning history / summarising prior turns / scoping retrieval
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What is your expected outcome after that fix — what specifically should change in the numbers?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Compare the three options: which one addresses the accumulation directly versus treating a symptom?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If session history is 8,000 tokens per request and output is 600, where is the highest ROI?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said you would fix the long response first. How much would that save if each response is 800 tokens but the session history is 9,000 tokens?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner prioritises output trimming over session pruning
socratic_bank.expected_response: Not much / less than pruning history / it depends
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So which fix produces the higher ROI on the evidence in front of you?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'If you could only make one change, which one addresses the largest token contributor?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Output trimming might save 200 tokens per response. History pruning might save 6,000. Which is the highest-ROI fix?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us use three steps only: read the number, name the pattern, choose one fix. What does the evidence tell you in step one?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner jumps to fixes without diagnosis
socratic_bank.expected_response: Some reading of the numbers
socratic_bank.if_correct: Walk through: 'Good. Step two: given that number, which bloat pattern does it suggest?' Then step three.
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Before step two, just read what the numbers say — no interpretation yet. What are the numbers?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Model the three steps explicitly with the learner, one step at a time, asking for their input at each stage.

M5.name: Instructions and Skills — Building the Two-File Architecture
M5.learning_objective: Design reusable instruction files and skills with clear triggers, workflow steps, output formats, and anti-pattern coverage.
M5.core_mental_model: What repeats becomes a system; reliable repeated behavior should not remain a one-off prompt.
M5.in_scope: Instruction/skill distinction, trigger precision, workflow, output discipline, anti-pattern awareness.
M5.out_of_scope: Full multi-agent orchestration, memory architecture, runtime MCP control.
M5.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: rewrite only the trigger condition and workflow so another engineer could reuse this without re-explaining the task.

concepts.name: Instruction File
concepts.summary: An instruction file (sometimes called copilot-instructions.md or a system prompt document) is a persistent artifact containing broad, stable guidance that governs the model's general behaviour across many tasks: its role, tone, scope boundaries, what it should always and never do.
concepts.why_it_matters: Without an instruction file, engineers restate broad guidance in every prompt — creating inconsistency and token waste. The instruction file makes stable behaviour reusable and maintainable.
concepts.when_to_use: When defining persistent agent behaviour, role, scope, and boundaries that apply across all tasks the agent performs.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not put task-specific logic, narrow triggers, or workflow steps in the instruction file. Those belong in skill files.
concepts.example: A code review agent's instruction file states: role (senior code reviewer), tone (direct, constructive), scope (only review files in the PR, not the whole repo), and boundaries (do not suggest architectural changes unless asked). These rules apply to every task.
concepts.non_example: Writing a separate long prompt for every code review request instead of defining the role and boundaries once in a persistent file.

concepts.name: Skill File
concepts.summary: A skill file is a reusable, task-specific artifact that defines a repeatable behaviour: what triggers it, the workflow steps it follows, the output format it produces, and the anti-patterns it avoids. A skill file is narrower than an instruction file and activates under specific conditions.
concepts.why_it_matters: Skill files turn repeated cognitive effort into system behaviour. Instead of writing the same prompt for code reviews, test generation, or documentation every time, the skill file encodes that behaviour once — consistently and reusably.
concepts.when_to_use: When a task is repeated across the team, when the same steps and output format are expected each time, when consistency across engineers matters.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not use a skill file for broad, always-on behaviour. A skill that 'always applies' is an instruction file, not a skill.
concepts.example: A skill file for 'PR security review' defines: trigger (when a PR touches authentication or payment code), workflow (check for injection risks, then auth bypass, then data exposure), output format (findings table with severity and line number), anti-patterns (do not flag style issues, do not restate the PR description).
concepts.non_example: Writing a skill file that says 'review code when asked'. That trigger is too vague to be reusable — it would activate for any code question.

concepts.name: Trigger Condition
concepts.summary: A trigger condition is the observable, specific event or state that causes a skill to activate. A good trigger names an exact action, request type, or file state — not a vague category. It must be clear enough that another engineer reading it can predict when the skill will fire.
concepts.why_it_matters: Vague triggers cause unreliable or unexpected activation. A trigger that says 'when needed for code' will fire too broadly or not at all — because no one can predict what counts as 'needed'.
concepts.when_to_use: When writing or reviewing a skill file. The trigger is the most critical element — a skill with a weak trigger cannot be trusted.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not write triggers that depend on mind-reading or context that is not in the request. The trigger must be observable from the request itself.
concepts.example: Strong trigger: 'When the engineer runs /review on a pull request that modifies files in /auth or /payments.' Weak trigger: 'When reviewing code that might have security issues.'
concepts.non_example: Writing 'activate when the user needs help' as a trigger. That is not observable — it relies on the model guessing intent.

concepts.name: Progressive Disclosure
concepts.summary: Progressive disclosure in context engineering means keeping only the information the model needs for the current step in context, revealing additional detail only as the workflow progresses. It prevents context overload by loading information just-in-time rather than all-at-once.
concepts.why_it_matters: Loading everything upfront fills the context with information the model will not use until step 5, while it is at step 1. Progressive disclosure keeps the context clean and relevant at every stage.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing multi-step workflows. When a task has sequential phases where early phases do not need the data required by later phases.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not apply progressive disclosure to always-load content like role and safety constraints. Those must be present from the start.
concepts.example: A document review skill first loads only the document title and structure. After the engineer confirms the review scope, it loads the relevant sections. Only if legal language is found does it load the legal review checklist. Each piece loads progressively.
concepts.non_example: Loading the full legal checklist, full document, and all review criteria at step 1 of a review that might not need legal review at all.

concepts.name: Anti-Pattern Coverage
concepts.summary: Anti-pattern coverage in a skill file is the explicit list of what the model should NOT do when the skill activates: which outputs to avoid, which topics to exclude, which failure modes to guard against. Anti-patterns are as important as positive workflow steps.
concepts.why_it_matters: Without anti-patterns, the model defaults to its broadest interpretation — which often includes the exact behaviours the team wants to prevent. Anti-patterns are the guardrails that keep a skill focused.
concepts.when_to_use: When writing or reviewing any skill file. Every skill should have at least two relevant anti-patterns that reflect real failure modes.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not write generic anti-patterns like 'do not be unhelpful'. Anti-patterns must be task-specific and tied to real failure modes observed in the workflow.
concepts.example: A test generation skill's anti-patterns: 'Do not generate tests for already-covered cases unless asked. Do not include test data that contains real customer identifiers. Do not suggest changes to the function under test.'
concepts.non_example: Leaving anti-patterns blank or writing 'do not make mistakes'. Generic anti-patterns provide no guardrails.

misconceptions.misconception: Skills are optional polish
misconceptions.why_wrong: Skills are not decorative — they are the mechanism that converts repeated human effort into reliable, consistent system behaviour. Without skills, every engineer recreates the same prompt logic independently, with variation and drift.
misconceptions.correct_view: Skill files are a core engineering practice for teams using AI assistants. They create consistency, reduce cognitive overhead, and enable reuse at scale.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'We could write skill files but our engineers know what to do — it is not worth the overhead.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If 10 engineers each write their own version of a code review prompt, how consistent will the review outputs be across the team? What happens when they onboard 5 new engineers?'

misconceptions.misconception: Longer instructions are always better
misconceptions.why_wrong: Longer instruction files and skill files become their own source of input bloat. A 5,000-token instruction file that could be 800 tokens wastes cost on every request and is harder to maintain.
misconceptions.correct_view: Instructions should be complete but minimal. Economy of instruction is a quality criterion — not laziness.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I keep adding more detail to the instruction file to make the agent more reliable.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If the instruction file grows to 10,000 tokens and is loaded on every request across 1,000 daily users, what is the monthly cost of the instruction file alone?'

misconceptions.misconception: Vague triggers are acceptable
misconceptions.why_wrong: Vague triggers produce unpredictable activation — the skill fires when it should not, or fails to fire when it should. This makes the system unreliable and the skill unusable for team-wide deployment.
misconceptions.correct_view: Trigger conditions must be observable, specific, and testable. A trigger that another engineer cannot predict from reading it is not production-ready.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'My trigger says when code review is needed — that should be clear enough.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'Could another engineer reading this trigger tell you in advance exactly when it will activate and when it will not? If not, what observable condition should replace it?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Your team writes a slightly different code review prompt every time. What problem does that create at scale?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening question to surface the motivation for skill files
socratic_bank.expected_response: Inconsistency / duplication / different outputs / harder to maintain
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What would it take to make that behaviour consistent across 50 engineers without asking each one to remember the rules?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'How does variation in the prompt affect the consistency of the review output?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If you wanted every engineer to get the same quality of review, what would need to be standardised?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Your skill trigger says 'when the engineer needs a code review'. What would another engineer need to know to predict when this skill activates?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner writes a vague trigger
socratic_bank.expected_response: They would need to know what counts as needing a review / it is too vague
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What observable condition — something visible in the request — should replace that?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Can you rewrite the trigger using an action you can see in the request, not an intent you have to guess?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What specific event, command, or file state would tell you with certainty that this skill should activate?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Your skill has a trigger and a workflow. What happens when the model follows the workflow but produces the wrong format every time?
socratic_bank.use_when: When output format is missing from the skill
socratic_bank.expected_response: It defaults to its own format / the output is inconsistent
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What is missing from the skill that would prevent that?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Where in the skill file would you add that instruction?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If you want the same output format every time this skill runs, where does that specification live?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said you do not need a skill file because the engineers know what to do. What happens when you onboard 10 new engineers next month?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner dismisses skill files as unnecessary overhead
socratic_bank.expected_response: They would have to learn the unwritten rules / inconsistency / knowledge in people not systems
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What is the cost of that knowledge living in people rather than in a reusable system artifact?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'How does tribal knowledge scale across a team that doubles in size?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If the senior engineer leaves, what happens to the prompting approach they have perfected over 6 months?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us build the skill one section at a time. What is the one task this skill should do — and only this task?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner writes an unfocused or over-broad skill
socratic_bank.expected_response: A specific task name
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good. Now — what specific observable condition should make that task activate?'
