M6.name: Seven Patterns for Advanced Token Optimization
M6.learning_objective: Apply advanced optimization patterns to reduce tokens while preserving relevance and answer quality.
M6.core_mental_model: Optimization is selective relevance preservation, not reduction for its own sake.
M6.in_scope: Pattern selection, trade-off reasoning, preservation/removal logic.
M6.out_of_scope: Full memory architecture, production deployment configuration, broad governance frameworks.
M6.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: choose exactly one optimization pattern for one bloated scenario and justify it in terms of waste removed and signal preserved.

concepts.name: Scoped Read Pattern
concepts.summary: The scoped read pattern retrieves only the relevant subset of a file or document rather than loading the entire artifact. Instead of reading a 2,000-line codebase file, the agent reads only the function or class relevant to the current task.
concepts.why_it_matters: Full file reads are one of the most common sources of input bloat in engineering agents. A scoped read pattern reduces input tokens by 80–95% on large files while preserving the information the model actually needs.
concepts.when_to_use: When an agent needs to read files, databases, or documents. When only a portion of the artifact is relevant to the current task.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not apply scoped reads when the full artifact is needed for the task — summarising or sampling when completeness is required produces incorrect outputs.
concepts.example: A dependency audit agent needs to check if a service imports a specific library. Instead of loading the full 800-line file, it reads only the import block (lines 1–20). Token cost drops from ~1,600 tokens to ~40 tokens.
concepts.non_example: Always reading full files 'to be safe'. Reading more than needed is never safer — it dilutes attention and inflates cost.

concepts.name: Search-Before-Read Pattern
concepts.summary: The search-before-read pattern locates the specific content needed before loading it — using a search, index lookup, or metadata check to identify the relevant subset before committing to a full read.
concepts.why_it_matters: Search-before-read prevents unnecessary full reads. It is the difference between knowing which chapter to read and reading the whole book to find one paragraph.
concepts.when_to_use: When working with large codebases, documentation sets, or databases where the relevant content is a small fraction of the whole.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Search-before-read requires an indexable or searchable structure. It cannot be applied to unstructured blobs without a retrieval layer.
concepts.example: Before reviewing a function, the agent searches for the function name across the codebase, identifies the file and line range, then reads only that range. No full file load occurs.
concepts.non_example: Skipping the search step and reading the full file to find the relevant function. This is the most common cause of input bloat in coding agents.

concepts.name: Output Trimming Pattern
concepts.summary: Output trimming is the pattern of instructing the model to remove ceremonial, redundant, or decorative content from its responses — preambles, restatements, summaries that repeat what was just said, and excessive caveats that add no information.
concepts.why_it_matters: Output tokens cost money and take time. In agentic pipelines, bloated output also becomes the next step's input — compounding the cost. Output trimming is the fastest win for reducing per-response cost.
concepts.when_to_use: When model responses consistently include preamble, restatement, or ceremonial language. When the output format specification is absent or weak.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not trim output so aggressively that necessary explanation, evidence, or reasoning is removed. Trimming is for padding, not substance.
concepts.example: Adding to a skill file's output format: 'Respond with findings only. No preamble, no restatement of the task, no closing summary. If no issues are found, respond with: No issues found.' Response length drops by 60%.
concepts.non_example: Adding 'be concise' to an instruction file and expecting it to hold. Vague brevity instructions are overridden by the model's default verbosity. Specific output format constraints are required.

concepts.name: MCP Sandboxing Pattern
concepts.summary: MCP sandboxing is the pattern of isolating raw tool outputs — large payloads from external tool calls, API responses, or database results — rather than injecting them directly into the model's working context. The raw output is stored separately; only a processed summary enters the context.
concepts.why_it_matters: Raw tool outputs can be enormous — a single API response or database query result can exceed 10,000 tokens. Injecting them directly into context fills the window with machine-formatted data the model must parse, rather than pre-processed signal.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing agents that call external tools, APIs, or databases. When tool outputs are large or variable in size.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Sandboxing requires a processing step between the tool call and context injection. It cannot be applied to tools whose raw output is directly needed for the model to reason — use judgment.
concepts.example: A tool call returns a 5,000-token JSON payload. The sandboxing pattern processes this into a 200-token structured summary before injecting it into context. The model reasons from the summary, not the raw payload.
concepts.non_example: Injecting full API responses into the model context because 'the model needs to see everything'. In most cases, a processed summary is more useful than raw data.

concepts.name: Query-First Retrieval Pattern
concepts.summary: Query-first retrieval is the pattern of formulating a precise retrieval query before fetching any content — ensuring that what is retrieved is directly relevant to the current need, rather than fetching broad content and relying on the model to filter it.
concepts.why_it_matters: Broad retrieval produces content the model must sift through in context — wasting tokens on irrelevant material. Query-first retrieval ensures that what enters context is already scoped to the task.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) flows, knowledge base lookups, or any pattern where content is fetched before the model responds.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Query-first retrieval requires a clear understanding of what is needed before retrieval. If the need is ambiguous, clarify with the user before retrieving.
concepts.example: Instead of retrieving all documentation about the payments API, the agent first formulates a query: 'authentication error codes for payments API v2'. Retrieval returns 3 relevant pages instead of 40.
concepts.non_example: Retrieving all documents tagged 'payments' and letting the model find the relevant section. Broad retrieval with in-context filtering wastes tokens and dilutes attention.

misconceptions.misconception: Less data is always better
misconceptions.why_wrong: Over-optimisation removes context the model needs to reason correctly. Removing necessary information to save tokens produces incorrect outputs that require more retries — costing more in the end.
misconceptions.correct_view: Optimisation is selective relevance preservation. The goal is removing waste while preserving signal — not minimising tokens indiscriminately.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I am going to cut everything I can to reduce tokens.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If you removed the function signature and error message from a debugging context to save 200 tokens, and the model then gave an incorrect answer requiring three retries, was the optimisation actually a saving?'

misconceptions.misconception: Output trimming solves all token problems
misconceptions.why_wrong: Output trimming addresses output bloat only. It does not fix input bloat (too much in the prompt) or session bloat (accumulated history). Applying output trimming to an input or session bloat problem produces minimal improvement.
misconceptions.correct_view: Each bloat type requires its own pattern. Output trimming is one of seven patterns — it is effective for its specific problem and ineffective for others.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'I added brevity instructions to my skill file — that should fix the token problem.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If the dominant waste in your session is 8,000 tokens of accumulated history, how much does output trimming help if each response is already only 300 tokens?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Your coding agent reads the entire 2,000-line service file every time someone asks about one function. What does that cost, and what is the risk?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening scenario for Module 6 patterns
socratic_bank.expected_response: High token cost / irrelevant content / attention dilution
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What pattern would reduce that cost while still giving the model what it needs?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'How much of that 2,000-line file does the model actually need to answer a question about one function?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What would you change about how the file is read?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You chose output trimming for this scenario. What is the dominant waste in a session where history has grown to 12,000 tokens and each response is 400 tokens?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner defaults to output trimming
socratic_bank.expected_response: The history is the dominant waste / output trimming is the wrong fix
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So which pattern addresses the actual dominant waste here — and why is output trimming not the highest-ROI choice?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Compare the savings: trimming 400-token responses versus pruning 12,000 tokens of history. Which has higher ROI?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Output trimming fixes output bloat. What type of bloat is the 12,000-token history?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You applied scoped reads. What signal must remain in context for the model to answer correctly — and what did you remove?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner applies a pattern — probe the trade-off
socratic_bank.expected_response: The relevant function and its dependencies must remain / removed unrelated code
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What is the risk if you scope the read too aggressively and remove a dependency the model needed?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'How do you know the subset you loaded is sufficient?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What would you expect to see in the output if you accidentally removed something the model needed?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said less data is always better. What happens if you scope the read so tightly that you exclude the error handler the model needed to diagnose the bug?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner over-applies optimisation
socratic_bank.expected_response: The model gives a wrong answer / it cannot diagnose without that context
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'So what is the actual goal of optimisation — fewer tokens, or the right tokens?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What is the minimum necessary context — and how is that different from the minimum possible context?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Optimisation that produces incorrect answers requiring three retries — is that actually saving tokens?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us use a five-step frame: symptom, pattern, preserved signal, removed waste, overuse risk. What is the symptom in this scenario?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner cannot match pattern to problem
socratic_bank.expected_response: Names the visible problem
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Good. Which of the seven patterns most directly addresses that symptom?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Walk through each step in sequence, asking for the learner's input at each stage before moving to the next.
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What does the session look like — slow, expensive, drifting? That is the symptom. Now let us name it precisely.'

M7.name: From Skills to Agents — The SDLC Transition
M7.learning_objective: Design agent architectures that distinguish skills from agents, specify memory types, control tool handling, define instruction structure, and apply governance constraints.
M7.core_mental_model: An agent is not a bigger prompt; it is a controlled system coordinating context, tools, memory, and governance over time.
M7.in_scope: Skill-vs-agent distinction, memory types, tool containment, instruction structure, governance-aware design.
M7.out_of_scope: Deep infrastructure implementation, custom connector internals, production admin operations.
M7.one_next_step_template: Your next step is: evaluate one agent design against memory type, tool handling, instruction structure, and governance, then propose one highest-value change.

concepts.name: Agent Architecture
concepts.summary: An agent architecture is a designed system that combines persistent instructions, a knowledge or tool layer, a memory model, and an orchestration logic to handle tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, or tool interactions — going beyond what a single prompt or skill file can achieve.
concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding agent architecture prevents engineers from building agents that are really just long prompts. An architecture requires explicit decisions about memory, tool handling, instruction scope, and governance — not just a bigger system prompt.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing a system that must handle multi-step tasks, maintain state across interactions, or coordinate multiple tools.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not call something an agent architecture if it is a single skill file with no memory or tool coordination. The term carries specific design obligations.
concepts.example: A code review agent architecture: instruction file (persistent role and governance), skill files (PR review, security review, test coverage check), working memory (current PR context), tool integration (GitHub API for file access), governance (scope boundary and fallback behaviour).
concepts.non_example: Calling a long system prompt an 'agent'. An agent has designed memory, tools, and orchestration — not just more instructions.

concepts.name: Working Memory
concepts.summary: Working memory in an agent is the context available within the current session — the active conversation, current tool outputs, and task-specific state that exists only for the duration of the interaction. When the session ends, working memory is cleared.
concepts.why_it_matters: Working memory must be actively managed — it fills up and degrades if unmanaged. Engineers designing agents need to know what belongs in working memory versus what should be persisted elsewhere.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing session-scoped state management. When deciding what the agent needs to remember within a task but not across tasks.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not mistake working memory for persistent memory. Information in working memory is lost when the session ends.
concepts.example: A PR review agent holds the current PR's diff, the engineer's scope instructions, and interim findings in working memory. These are needed for the current review and discarded after. The team's coding standards are not in working memory — they are loaded from persistent storage on demand.
concepts.non_example: Designing an agent that expects to remember a user's preferences across separate sessions using working memory. That requires persistent memory, not session memory.

concepts.name: Persistent Memory
concepts.summary: Persistent memory is information the agent retains across sessions — user preferences, project settings, historical decisions, and learned patterns that should be available the next time the agent is used, without being re-stated.
concepts.why_it_matters: Without explicit persistent memory design, teams either lose valuable cross-session context or accidentally carry sensitive data further than intended. Persistent memory requires deliberate decisions about what to retain, how long to retain it, and who can access it.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing agents that serve the same users repeatedly, where cross-session learning or preference retention adds value.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not default to persistent memory for everything. Persistent memory carries governance obligations — data retention, access control, and update mechanisms.
concepts.example: A code quality agent persistently remembers: this team prefers functional programming patterns, their test framework is Jest, and they have a known exception to the security policy for internal admin routes. This context loads automatically without the engineer restating it each session.
concepts.non_example: Storing every session's full conversation in persistent memory. Persistent memory should hold distilled, reusable facts — not raw transcripts.

concepts.name: Temporal Memory
concepts.summary: Temporal memory is information that is valid for a limited time and must be refreshed or discarded when it expires. Cached API schemas, current sprint goals, today's deployment status, and time-sensitive configuration values are temporal — they change and become dangerous if remembered too long.
concepts.why_it_matters: Temporal memory that is not refreshed becomes misleading. An agent that confidently uses a cached API schema from three weeks ago will generate incorrect guidance when the API has changed.
concepts.when_to_use: When identifying what type of information to persist. Any fact that has a validity window belongs in temporal memory with an expiry policy.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not treat temporal memory the same as persistent memory. Temporal memory requires an expiry or refresh mechanism — not just a store.
concepts.example: An agent caches the current sprint's open tickets as temporal memory. The cache is valid for 4 hours. After 4 hours, the agent refreshes from the ticket system before answering questions about sprint status.
concepts.non_example: Persisting today's deployment status indefinitely. Deployment status changes multiple times a day — it is temporal, not persistent.

concepts.name: Governance in Agent Design
concepts.summary: Governance in agent design is the set of explicit constraints, safety rules, scope boundaries, fallback behaviours, and accountability mechanisms built into the agent's architecture — not assumed or left to the model's defaults.
concepts.why_it_matters: Internal agents are not exempt from governance. An agent that handles code, data, or user interactions without explicit governance constraints is a liability — especially in regulated industries or where the agent's outputs have real-world consequences.
concepts.when_to_use: When designing any agent that will be used in a production or team context. Governance is not optional for production agents.
concepts.when_not_to_use: Do not assume governance is handled by the underlying model. Governance must be explicitly designed into the instruction architecture.
concepts.example: A code review agent's governance layer: only review code in the current PR (scope boundary), do not suggest changes to test infrastructure without a human in the loop (safety constraint), if asked to review sensitive payment code fall back to a human reviewer (fallback behaviour), log all security findings for audit (accountability).
concepts.non_example: Saying 'governance is the model's responsibility'. The model's defaults are not governance. Governance is designed, explicit, and auditable.

misconceptions.misconception: An agent is just a longer prompt
misconceptions.why_wrong: A prompt has no memory, no tool coordination, no state management, and no governance layer. An agent is a designed system with explicit decisions across all of these dimensions. Equating them produces architectures that are actually just fragile long prompts.
misconceptions.correct_view: Agent design requires explicit decisions about memory type, tool handling, instruction structure, and governance. These cannot be substituted with prompt length.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'My agent is really just a very detailed system prompt with all the instructions.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What happens to your system when the task takes 10 turns and requires three tool calls? Does your design handle state, tool containment, and fallback — or does it rely on the model figuring it out?'

misconceptions.misconception: Governance only matters for public-facing agents
misconceptions.why_wrong: Internal agents handle real code, real data, and real decisions. Governance failures in internal tools are just as consequential as in public tools — they affect code quality, security posture, and team trust.
misconceptions.correct_view: Governance is required for any agent that handles consequential tasks, regardless of whether it faces internal or external users.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'This agent is just for our team — we do not need formal governance constraints.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'If your internal code review agent misses a critical security vulnerability because its scope boundary was not explicit, who is responsible? What governance mechanism would have prevented that?'

misconceptions.misconception: Working memory and persistent memory are the same
misconceptions.why_wrong: Working memory exists only for the current session and is cleared when the session ends. Persistent memory survives across sessions. Using working memory for cross-session state causes data loss; using persistent memory for session-only state creates privacy and governance risks.
misconceptions.correct_view: Memory type selection is a design decision with real consequences. The right memory type depends on how long the information needs to remain valid and who should be able to access it.
misconceptions.typical_phrase: 'The agent remembers what we discussed — I do not need to set up separate storage for preferences.'
misconceptions.correction_strategy: Ask: 'What happens to the preferences the agent learned in today's session when the engineer starts a new session tomorrow? If they are gone, was that by design or by accident?'

socratic_bank.prompt: A team calls their system an agent. It has a very long system prompt and no tool configuration, no memory design, and no governance layer. What makes something an agent rather than a long prompt?
socratic_bank.use_when: Opening question to surface agent vs prompt distinction
socratic_bank.expected_response: Memory / tools / state / orchestration / governance
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'Given that list, what would you say is missing from what this team built?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What decisions does an agent have to make that a static prompt cannot make?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What does an agent do between user turns that a prompt does not?'

socratic_bank.prompt: The agent needs to remember a user's coding preferences. Should that live in working memory or persistent memory — and why?
socratic_bank.use_when: After learner understands memory types exist
socratic_bank.expected_response: Persistent memory — preferences survive sessions
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What would happen to those preferences if they were stored in working memory and the user started a new session?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'How long do preferences need to remain valid — for this session only, or across many sessions?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'What is the governance implication of storing user preferences in persistent memory?'

socratic_bank.prompt: The agent calls an external API and receives a 6,000-token JSON response. Where does that response go, and what is the risk if it goes directly into working context?
socratic_bank.use_when: To surface tool containment and sandboxing need
socratic_bank.expected_response: It fills the context / dilutes relevance / expensive
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What pattern would prevent the raw payload from polluting the working context?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'What would you extract from that 6,000-token response to put in context instead?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'If the agent does this on every turn across a 10-turn session, what happens to the context?'

socratic_bank.prompt: You said governance is unnecessary for an internal tool. What happens if the agent's scope boundary is not explicit and it begins reviewing files outside the current PR?
socratic_bank.use_when: When learner dismisses governance for internal use
socratic_bank.expected_response: It could review sensitive code / cause security issues / produce irrelevant feedback
socratic_bank.if_correct: Ask: 'What explicit governance rule would have prevented that? And is that rule the model's default, or does it need to be designed?'
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Internal use does not mean low stakes — what is the consequence of an unscoped code review agent accessing production secrets?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Ask: 'Is the model's default behaviour the same as a governance policy? What is the difference?'

socratic_bank.prompt: Let us evaluate this agent design against four criteria: memory type, tool handling, instruction structure, and governance. Score each one: Pass, Needs work, or Missing. Start with memory — what do you see?
socratic_bank.use_when: Recovery when learner cannot evaluate an agent design
socratic_bank.expected_response: Some attempt to assess memory
socratic_bank.if_correct: Move through each criterion in sequence after the learner scores each one.
socratic_bank.if_partial: Ask: 'Set aside everything else. Look only at the memory design. Is there an explicit statement of what is session-local versus what persists?'
socratic_bank.if_incorrect: Model the scoring of one criterion explicitly, then ask the learner to score the remaining three independently.
